hadean.etymology: Named for Hades. The eon is informal: the crust was melted and cratered so thoroughly that almost no rock remains to put a golden spike in.
hadean.climate: The planet was molten, then cooled under a heavy steam atmosphere. Oceans may have condensed before 4,000 Ma. Impacts, including the one that made the Moon, dominated the surface.
hadean.life: No undisputed fossils. Any life would have been microscopic and is inferred from chemistry, not from shells or bones.
hadean.ending: The chart places the top at 4,031 Ma, the base of the Archean, a round Global Standard Stratigraphic Age rather than a golden spike.

archean.etymology: From Greek archaios, ancient. The eon of the first preserved continents and the oldest widely accepted traces of life.
archean.climate: The Sun was fainter than today, yet liquid water was widespread. The air had almost no free oxygen. Heat flow was high and plates were smaller and faster.
archean.life: Microbial mats and stromatolites. By the late Archean, cyanobacteria were releasing oxygen that had not yet filled the atmosphere.
archean.ending: It ends at 2,500 Ma, the round age chosen for the base of the Proterozoic, as oxygen began to accumulate in earnest.

eoarchean.etymology: Greek eos, dawn, plus Archean: the oldest Archean era.
eoarchean.climate: A hot, airless-of-oxygen world with small continental nuclei and a heavy bombardment still tapering off. The oldest surviving rocks, in Canada and Greenland, are this age.
eoarchean.life: Possible chemical traces of life in the oldest sediments. Nothing with a skeleton, and nothing you could see without a microscope.
eoarchean.ending: The top is the round age 3,600 Ma, the base of the Paleoarchean.

paleoarchean.climate: Stable patches of continental crust grew, including the Kaapvaal and Pilbara blocks. Seas were warm and the air was still anoxic.
paleoarchean.life: The best early stromatolites, in Western Australia and South Africa, are this age. Life was microbial mats in shallow water.
paleoarchean.ending: It ends at the round age 3,200 Ma.

mesoarchean.climate: Continents continued to thicken. The climate stayed warm and free of an oxygen-rich atmosphere, with widespread shallow seas on granite-greenstone crust.
mesoarchean.life: Stromatolites spread. Molecular evidence suggests the ancestors of later bacterial groups were already distinct, still without animals or plants.
mesoarchean.ending: It ends at the round age 2,800 Ma.

neoarchean.etymology: Greek neos, new, plus Archean: the last Archean era.
neoarchean.climate: Large continental blocks assembled. Oxygen from photosynthesis was still soaked up by iron and other sinks, so the air stayed almost oxygen-free until the very end.
neoarchean.life: Microbial life was abundant. Banded iron formations record dissolved iron reacting with the first free oxygen in seawater.
neoarchean.ending: It ends at 2,500 Ma, where the Proterozoic and the long rise of oxygen begin.

proterozoic.etymology: Greek proteros and zoikos, earlier life. The eon between the Archean and the first abundant animal shells.
proterozoic.climate: Oxygen rose in steps, the planet froze over at least twice near the end, and modern-style continents drifted into and out of supercontinents.
proterozoic.life: Eukaryotic cells appear, then multicellular algae and, at the very end, the first animals. For most of the eon the fossil record is still microbial.
proterozoic.ending: It ends at 538.8 Ma, the golden spike at the base of the Cambrian, when complex trace fossils and the first small shells become the rule.

paleoproterozoic.climate: The Great Oxidation Event filled the air with a little oxygen and turned the continents red. The Huronian glaciations, possibly the first Snowball Earth, fall early in the era.
paleoproterozoic.life: Aerobic metabolism became possible. Eukaryotic cells probably originated. Fossils are still mostly stromatolites and chemical signatures.
paleoproterozoic.ending: It ends at the round age 1,600 Ma, the base of the Mesoproterozoic.

mesoproterozoic.climate: A long, relatively stable stretch. The supercontinent Columbia broke up and Rodinia later began to assemble. Oxygen stayed modest and the climate has no confirmed snowball.
mesoproterozoic.life: Eukaryotic algae and the first widely accepted multicellular organisms. Sexual reproduction and cells with nuclei were established. Animals had not yet appeared.
mesoproterozoic.ending: It ends at the round age 1,000 Ma, the base of the Tonian.

neoproterozoic.etymology: The new Proterozoic, 1,000 Ma to 538.8 Ma. Its base is a round age; the Ediacaran inside it has a golden spike.
neoproterozoic.climate: Rodinia rifted apart. Twice, in the Cryogenian, ice reached the tropics. After the ice, continents sat scattered and sea level rose.
neoproterozoic.life: The era of the first animals: sponges and the soft-bodied Ediacaran biota, then the threshold of the Cambrian explosion.
neoproterozoic.ending: It ends at the Cambrian golden spike, 538.8 Ma, at Fortune Head in Newfoundland.

siderian.etymology: Greek sideros, iron, for the peak of banded iron formations.
siderian.climate: Oxygen from photosynthesis finally overwhelmed the chemical sinks. Iron rusted out of the oceans and the first widespread ice ages of the Proterozoic arrived.
siderian.life: Cyanobacterial mats kept building stromatolites. Complex animals were still far in the future.
siderian.ending: The top is the round age 2,300 Ma. These Precambrian periods are defined by Global Standard Stratigraphic Ages, not golden spikes.

rhyacian.etymology: Greek rhyax, a stream of lava, for the great igneous provinces of this time.
rhyacian.climate: After the Huronian ice, the climate warmed. Huge eruptions and the growth of continental crust mark the period. Oxygen continued its uneven rise.
rhyacian.life: Life stayed microbial. The Gunflint-type communities of bacteria and early eukaryotes belong in this broad stretch of time.
rhyacian.ending: It ends at the round age 2,050 Ma.

orosirian.etymology: Greek orosira, mountain range, for a cluster of mountain-building episodes and for the giant Vredefort and Sudbury impacts.
orosirian.climate: Continents collided and thickened. The atmosphere held some oxygen, and the climate was warmer than the glacial Siderian.
orosirian.life: The fossil record is still mats and microscopic cells. The oldest widely discussed eukaryotic fossils fall near this part of the Proterozoic.
orosirian.ending: It ends at the round age 1,800 Ma.

statherian.etymology: Greek statheros, stable, because many cratons were unusually quiet.
statherian.climate: Platforms of continental crust sat still under broad shallow seas. Oxygen remained low by modern standards and ice sheets were not the main story.
statherian.life: Stromatolites were widespread. Multicellular life had not taken over the seafloor.
statherian.ending: It ends at the round age 1,600 Ma, the base of the Calymmian.

calymmian.etymology: Greek calymma, a cover, for platform covers of sediment on the older cratons.
calymmian.climate: Broad, quiet continental shelves. The supercontinent Columbia was breaking up. No snowball glaciation is known.
calymmian.life: Eukaryotic microfossils become more varied. Acritarchs, the organic-walled cysts of plankton, are the usual fossils.
calymmian.ending: It ends at the round age 1,400 Ma.

ectasian.etymology: Greek ectasis, extension, for the rifts that stretched the continents.
ectasian.climate: Basins opened as Columbia finished breaking up. Climate stayed mild enough that glacial deposits are scarce.
ectasian.life: Acritarchs and algal fossils continued. The first possible red-algae fossils are discussed from rocks of about this age.
ectasian.ending: It ends at the round age 1,200 Ma.

stenian.etymology: Greek stenos, narrow, for the narrow belts of metamorphism and mountain building as Rodinia assembled.
stenian.climate: Continents were gathering into Rodinia. The climate was not glacial. Oxygen remained well below modern levels.
stenian.life: Still a microbial and algal world. The famous Hunting Formation and similar rocks preserve early multicellular algae.
stenian.ending: It ends at the round age 1,000 Ma, the base of the Tonian.

tonian.etymology: Greek tonos, stretch, for the rifting of Rodinia.
tonian.climate: Rodinia began to split. The climate cooled toward the Cryogenian snowballs. The end of the period, about 720 Ma, is still approximate.
tonian.life: Acritarchs diversified, then many of them vanished. Molecular clocks and a few fossils put the first animals, including sponges, in or just after this period.
tonian.ending: It ends at the approximate age of the first Cryogenian glaciation, about 720 Ma. No golden spike has been ratified.

cryogenian.etymology: Greek cryos, ice. Both boundaries are still approximate.
cryogenian.climate: The Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations ran ice to the equator. Sea level fell, then the ice melted in sudden warmings. Continents sat in the wreckage of Rodinia.
cryogenian.life: Life retreated to refuges. Algae and microbes persisted. Sponges and other simple animals were present by the late Cryogenian.
cryogenian.ending: It ends with the close of the Marinoan glaciation, about 635 Ma, at the base of the Ediacaran.

ediacaran.etymology: Named for the Ediacara Hills in South Australia. This is the first Precambrian period with a golden spike, in the Flinders Ranges.
ediacaran.climate: After the snowballs, seas rose and the climate was generally mild until a cooler spell near the end. Continents were scattered, with shallow shelves around Laurentia, Baltica, and Gondwana.
ediacaran.life: The Ediacaran biota: soft-bodied fronds, discs, and quilted organisms, plus the first burrows. Cloudina and other small shells appear late. Dickinsonia and rangeomorphs have no exact modern match.
ediacaran.ending: It ends at 538.8 Ma, the Cambrian golden spike, where complex burrows of Treptichnus pedum take over from the Ediacaran assemblages.

phanerozoic.etymology: Greek phaneros and zoikos, visible life. The eon of animals with shells, bones, and teeth.
phanerozoic.climate: From 538.8 Ma to today: ice ages and greenhouses, the assembly and breakup of Pangaea, and sea level that has stood both far above and far below the modern shore.
phanerozoic.life: Essentially every familiar group of animals and plants arises here, from trilobites and forests to dinosaurs and humans.
phanerozoic.ending: It has not ended. The right-hand edge of the chart is the present.

paleozoic.etymology: Greek palaios and zoikos, old life. The era of trilobites, coal forests, and the first animals on land.
paleozoic.climate: Continents gathered from a scattered Cambrian world into the supercontinent Pangaea. Climate swung from warm seaways to the ice ages of the Ordovician and the Carboniferous.
paleozoic.life: The Cambrian explosion, the first reefs of animals, jawed fishes, forests, insects, and the first amniotes that could lay eggs on dry ground.
paleozoic.ending: It ends at 251.902 Ma in the end-Permian mass extinction, the largest in the fossil record.

mesozoic.etymology: Greek mesos and zoikos, middle life. Often called the Age of Dinosaurs, though the seas were just as distinctive.
mesozoic.climate: Pangaea split. For much of the era the climate was warm and ice-free, and shallow seas spread over the continents.
mesozoic.life: Dinosaurs, pterosaurs, marine reptiles, and the first birds and mammals. Ammonites filled the seas. Flowering plants took over late in the era.
mesozoic.ending: It ends at 66 Ma with the Chicxulub impact and the end-Cretaceous extinction.

cenozoic.etymology: Greek kainos and zoikos, recent life. The era of mammals, birds, grasses, and the ice ages.
cenozoic.climate: Continents moved into their modern places. Antarctica froze, then the northern ice sheets came and went. Sea level fell overall as ice grew.
cenozoic.life: Mammals and birds diversified into the niches dinosaurs left. Whales returned to the sea, grasses spread, and in the last fraction of the era, humans appeared.
cenozoic.ending: It is the current era. It runs from 66 Ma to the present.

cambrian.etymology: From Cambria, the Latin name for Wales, where early rocks of this age were studied.
cambrian.climate: Continents sat mostly in the southern hemisphere, with Laurentia on the equator. Sea level rose through the period and flooded the shelves. The climate was generally warm, with no confirmed ice age.
cambrian.life: The Cambrian explosion: trilobites, brachiopods, molluscs, echinoderms, and the stem relatives of vertebrates appear in a few tens of millions of years. Anomalocaris and the Burgess Shale fauna sit in the middle of the period.
cambrian.ending: It ends at 486.85 Ma. Several Cambrian animal groups were already in decline; the Ordovician then rebuilt diversity in a different style.

ordovician.etymology: Named for the Ordovices, a people of Roman-age Wales.
ordovician.climate: Sea level was among the highest of the Paleozoic, and warm shallow seas covered much of North America and Baltica. Gondwana drifted over the south pole, and the period ended in a sharp ice age.
ordovician.life: The Great Ordovician Biodiversification: brachiopods, bryozoans, crinoids, and graptolites filled the shelves. Jawless fishes were present. The first tentative plants may have reached freshwater.
ordovician.ending: It ends at 443.1 Ma in the end-Ordovician mass extinction, tied to the Hirnantian glaciation.

silurian.etymology: Named for the Silures, a people of the Welsh borderland, where Roderick Murchison studied the rocks.
silurian.climate: After the Ordovician ice, seas rose again and the climate warmed. Small continents sat near the equator, and reefs returned.
silurian.life: Coral-stromatoporoid reefs, giant sea scorpions, and the first jawed fishes. Vascular plants and the first animals moved onto land in a small way.
silurian.ending: It ends at 419.62 Ma. There is no mass extinction at the boundary, which is drawn on a change in graptolites at the base of the Devonian.

devonian.climate: The climate was warm and the sea stood high. Euramerica was assembling as Laurentia and Baltica collided. Forests appeared and began to change rivers and soils.
devonian.life: Often called the Age of Fishes: placoderms, sharks, and lobe-finned fishes, including Tiktaalik. The first forests of Archaeopteris, the first insects, and the first amphibians.
devonian.ending: It ends at 358.86 Ma. The Late Devonian extinction, in two pulses, had already dismantled the reefs and many fish groups.

carboniferous.etymology: Latin for coal-bearing. The coal is the buried peat of tropical swamp forests.
carboniferous.climate: Oxygen was high, ice grew on Gondwana, and sea level rose and fell with the glaciers. Euramerica sat on the equator under rainforests; the southern continents were cold.
carboniferous.life: Lycopod scale trees, giant griffinflies and millipedes, the first amniotes, and a huge diversity of sharks and ray-finned fishes. Amphibians were large and common.
carboniferous.ending: It ends at 298.9 Ma as the climate dried toward the Permian and the great coal swamps shrank. There is no Big Five extinction at this boundary.

permian.etymology: Named for the city of Perm, Russia, where Roderick Murchison named the rocks in 1841.
permian.climate: Pangaea was assembled. The interior of the supercontinent was dry and seasonal. Ice on Gondwana melted early, and the later Permian was hot.
permian.life: Sail-backed synapsids such as Dimetrodon, then the therapsids that lead toward mammals. Conifer and seed-fern floras replaced the coal swamps. In the sea, brachiopods, ammonoids, and reefs flourished until the end.
permian.ending: It ends at 251.902 Ma in the end-Permian mass extinction, caused largely by the Siberian Traps eruptions.

triassic.etymology: Named in Germany for a threefold stack of rocks: Buntsandstein, Muschelkalk, and Keuper.
triassic.climate: Pangaea still held together. The interior was arid, with red beds and salt. The climate was hot, and there is no confirmed polar ice. The Atlantic had not yet opened.
triassic.life: Life rebuilt after the end-Permian disaster. Lystrosaurus spread across the world, then archosaurs, the first dinosaurs, the first mammals, and marine reptiles. Conifers and ferns covered the land.
triassic.ending: It ends at 201.4 Ma in the end-Triassic extinction, linked to eruptions as the central Atlantic began to open.

jurassic.etymology: Named for the Jura Mountains on the French-Swiss border.
jurassic.climate: Pangaea split into Laurasia and Gondwana and the Atlantic began to open. The climate was warm and humid compared with the Triassic, and shallow seas flooded Europe.
jurassic.life: Dinosaurs became the dominant large land animals. The first birds, including Archaeopteryx, appear late in the period. Ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs, and ammonites filled the seas. Cycads and conifers were the common trees.
jurassic.ending: It ends at 143.1 Ma. There is no Big Five extinction here. The boundary with the Cretaceous is still not fixed by a golden spike, and the age is an estimate.

cretaceous.etymology: From Latin creta, chalk, for the chalk cliffs of Europe.
cretaceous.climate: Continents moved toward their modern outlines. For long stretches the climate was a greenhouse, and high sea level drowned the continents, including the Western Interior Seaway of North America.
cretaceous.life: Dinosaurs, including Tyrannosaurus and Triceratops, and the flowering plants. Mosasaurs, ammonites, and giant sea turtles in the chalk seas. Birds diversified. Mammals stayed mostly small.
cretaceous.ending: It ends at 66 Ma in the end-Cretaceous extinction, when the Chicxulub impact, on top of Deccan volcanism, closed the Mesozoic.

paleogene.etymology: Greek palaios and genos, old-born: the older part of the Cenozoic, once lumped into the Tertiary.
paleogene.climate: The climate started very warm and ended with the first big Antarctic ice. Continents were close to their modern places. India was closing on Asia, and the Atlantic was widening.
paleogene.life: Mammals diversified into the large-animal roles dinosaurs had held. Whales, horses, and primates appear. Forests reached the poles in the early Eocene, then retreated.
paleogene.ending: It ends at 23.04 Ma. The boundary is a plankton turnover and a shift toward the modern ocean, not a mass extinction.

neogene.climate: The climate cooled in steps. Grasslands spread as forests thinned. The Himalaya and the Andes rose, the Mediterranean dried and refilled, and the Isthmus of Panama closed near the end.
neogene.life: Horses, elephants, apes, and grazing mammals diversified. Whales were modern in outline. In Africa, the human lineage split from the other apes.
neogene.ending: It ends at 2.58 Ma, where northern-hemisphere ice sheets become the dominant climate cycle and the Quaternary begins.

quaternary.etymology: The fourth division in an old scheme that counted Primary, Secondary, and Tertiary before it. The name stuck.
quaternary.climate: Ice sheets repeatedly covered northern North America and Europe. Sea level swung by more than 100 metres between glacial and interglacial stages. The continents were already where they are now.
quaternary.life: Mammoths, ground sloths, and other megafauna, then modern humans. We are still in the Quaternary. The Holocene, and inside it the Meghalayan, is the current age.
quaternary.ending: It has not ended. The base, 2.58 Ma, is a golden spike marking the start of the ice-age world.

terreneuvian.etymology: Named for Terre-Neuve, the French name of Newfoundland, where the Cambrian golden spike is set.
terreneuvian.climate: Warm shallow seas on the margins of Laurentia and Gondwana. No ice sheets are known.
terreneuvian.life: Small shells and the first complex burrows. Trilobites had not yet appeared. This is the opening chapter of the Cambrian explosion.
terreneuvian.ending: It ends near 521 Ma, an approximate age, at the base of Series 2.

fortunian.etymology: Named for Fortune Head, Newfoundland, the golden spike of the Cambrian and of the Phanerozoic.
fortunian.climate: A warm world of shallow shelves. The spike itself is a point in a sea-cliff where the burrow Treptichnus pedum becomes common.
fortunian.life: The first small shelly fossils and deeper, more complicated burrows. No trilobites yet.
fortunian.ending: The top, about 529 Ma, is approximate. The next stage is still unnamed.

cambrian-stage-2.etymology: A placeholder. The International Commission has not yet ratified a formal name or a golden spike.
cambrian-stage-2.climate: Warm shelves continued. Archaeocyath sponges began to build the first animal reefs.
cambrian-stage-2.life: Small shelly fossils diversified. The famous Chengjiang and Burgess animals were still in the future.
cambrian-stage-2.ending: It ends near 521 Ma. Both bounds are approximate, which is why the stage is still a number.

cambrian-series-2.etymology: A placeholder epoch. It will get a formal name when its base is fixed by a golden spike.
cambrian-series-2.climate: Warm, rising seas. Reefs of archaeocyath sponges spread through the tropics.
cambrian-series-2.life: Trilobites appear at the base of Stage 3 and quickly become the common fossils. Early relatives of arthropods and the first chordate-like animals are known from Chengjiang, in south China.
cambrian-series-2.ending: It ends near 506.5 Ma. Archaeocyath reefs collapsed around this time, a smaller extinction sometimes called the Botomian event.

cambrian-stage-3.etymology: Still unnamed. The expected marker is the first appearance of trilobites.
cambrian-stage-3.climate: Warm tropical shelves. Archaeocyath reefs were growing.
cambrian-stage-3.life: The oldest trilobites, and at Chengjiang a soft-bodied fauna of early arthropods, worms, and animals close to the vertebrate line.
cambrian-stage-3.ending: The top, about 514.5 Ma, is approximate.

cambrian-stage-4.etymology: Still unnamed. It holds the later part of the trilobite diversification and the decline of the archaeocyath reefs.
cambrian-stage-4.climate: Sea level stayed high. The climate remained warm, without polar ice sheets.
cambrian-stage-4.life: Trilobites of the redlichiid and olenellid groups were widespread. Reefs of archaeocyath sponges reached their peak and then failed.
cambrian-stage-4.ending: It ends near 506.5 Ma at the base of the Miaolingian, close to the extinction that removed the archaeocyath reefs.

miaolingian.etymology: Named for the Miaoling Mountains in Guizhou, China.
miaolingian.climate: Broad warm seas. The Burgess Shale and similar lagerstätten preserve animals that lived on muddy shelves below the reach of storms.
miaolingian.life: Trilobites, anomalocaridids, and the stem groups of many living phyla. The Burgess Shale, about 508 Ma, is conventionally placed in the Wuliuan, at the start of this epoch.
miaolingian.ending: It ends near 497 Ma. The bounds are still approximate even though the base has a golden spike.

wuliuan.etymology: Named for Wuliu-Zengjiayan in Guizhou, the golden-spike section.
wuliuan.climate: Warm muddy shelves and carbonate banks. Sea level was high enough to drown many cratons.
wuliuan.life: A diverse trilobite fauna and, in the Burgess Shale of Canada, soft-bodied predators such as Anomalocaris. The gallery image of Anomalocaris belongs here.
wuliuan.ending: It ends near 504.5 Ma, an approximate age, at the base of the Drumian.

drumian.etymology: Named for the Drum Mountains of Utah.
drumian.climate: Similar warm shelves. A pulse of extinction among trilobites, the drumian biomere boundary, sits near the base.
drumian.life: Trilobites recovered with new families. Sponges and early echinoderms were common on the seafloor.
drumian.ending: The top, about 500.5 Ma, is approximate.

guzhangian.climate: Warm seas continued, with trilobite faunas turning over on the shallow platforms of Laurentia.
guzhangian.life: Polymerid trilobites and the last of several Cambrian reef communities. Soft-bodied faunas of this age are rarer than the Burgess Shale.
guzhangian.ending: It ends near 497 Ma at the base of the Furongian, another trilobite extinction and a carbon-isotope swing.

furongian.etymology: Named for Furong, the lotus, a traditional emblem of Hunan, where the golden spike is set.
furongian.climate: Sea level fluctuated. Several short extinctions of trilobites, called biomeres, punctuate the epoch. The climate stayed mostly warm.
furongian.life: Trilobite faunas dominated by olenids in deeper water. Conodonts, the tiny tooth-like fossils of jawless vertebrates, become useful clocks.
furongian.ending: It ends at 486.85 Ma, the base of the Ordovician, at a golden spike in Newfoundland.

paibian.etymology: Named for Paibi, Hunan, the golden-spike section.
paibian.climate: A large swing in carbon isotopes, the SPICE event, records a shake-up of the ocean. Shelves were still warm.
paibian.life: A sharp extinction of shallow-water trilobites at the base, followed by a new fauna. This is one of the Cambrian biomere events.
paibian.ending: The top, about 494.2 Ma, is approximate.

jiangshanian.climate: The ocean was still recovering from the SPICE carbon event. Climate remained warm and ice-free.
jiangshanian.life: Olenid trilobites in the deep water and a thinner fauna on the shelves. Conodonts continued to diversify.
jiangshanian.ending: The top, about 491 Ma, is approximate. The next stage is not yet named.

cambrian-stage-10.etymology: The last Cambrian age, still a number. Its golden spike has not been ratified. A conodont, Eoconodontus notchpeakensis, is the leading candidate for the marker.
cambrian-stage-10.climate: Warm shelves with a few cooler pulses. Sea level was restless just before the Ordovician.
cambrian-stage-10.life: The last Cambrian trilobite assemblages. The fauna was already thinning before the Ordovician radiation.
cambrian-stage-10.ending: It ends at 486.85 Ma at the golden spike of the Tremadocian, the base of the Ordovician.

early-ordovician.etymology: The Early Ordovician, called the Lower Ordovician when the talk is about the rocks rather than the time.
early-ordovician.climate: Warm seas were rising onto the continents. Gondwana carried the south pole, but the great ice age was still far ahead.
early-ordovician.life: Graptolites became common floating fossils. The first reefs of bryozoans and stromatoporoids got started. Diversity was climbing toward the great Ordovician radiation.
early-ordovician.ending: It ends at 471.3 Ma, the base of the Dapingian.

tremadocian.etymology: Named for Tremadoc in north Wales.
tremadocian.climate: A warm transgression flooded the shelves after the late Cambrian. Polar ice had not yet gathered.
tremadocian.life: Planktonic graptolites appear and spread worldwide. Trilobites and linguliform brachiopods were the common seafloor animals.
tremadocian.ending: It ends at 477.1 Ma at a golden spike marked by the graptolite Tetragraptus approximatus.

floian.etymology: Named for Flo, in south Sweden, near the Diabasbrottet golden spike.
floian.climate: Seas continued to rise. Shallow tropical carbonates spread across Laurentia.
floian.life: Graptolite faunas diversified. Conodonts and trilobites mark a further step in the Ordovician radiation.
floian.ending: It ends at 471.3 Ma, the base of the Dapingian.

middle-ordovician.etymology: The middle epoch of the Ordovician. Its base is the Dapingian golden spike.
middle-ordovician.climate: The climate was warm and sea level high. The Taconic mountains were beginning to rise along the margin of Laurentia as an island arc collided.
middle-ordovician.life: This is the heart of the Great Ordovician Biodiversification. Brachiopods, crinoids, and bryozoans built complex seafloor communities.
middle-ordovician.ending: It ends at 458.2 Ma, the base of the Sandbian.

dapingian.etymology: Named for Daping, a village near the golden spike at Huanghuachang, Yichang, China.
dapingian.climate: A short, warm age. Sea level was high and the shelves were lime-rich.
dapingian.life: A jump in diversity of brachiopods and graptolites. The great Ordovician radiation is underway in earnest.
dapingian.ending: It ends at 469.4 Ma, after only about two million years, at the base of the Darriwilian.

darriwilian.climate: Warm greenhouse shelves. Mountain building along eastern Laurentia was shedding sand into the interior seas.
darriwilian.life: The peak of the Ordovician radiation in many groups. Nautiloid cephalopods were the large predators. Jawless fishes are known from bone beds.
darriwilian.ending: It ends at 458.2 Ma at the base of the Sandbian.

late-ordovician.etymology: The Late Ordovician, a long warm stretch that ends in a brief, brutal ice age.
late-ordovician.climate: For most of the epoch, seas were high and the climate warm. Gondwana then drifted across the south pole and ice sheets grew in the Hirnantian.
late-ordovician.life: Rich brachiopod and coral faunas, graptolite plankton, and the first clear spores of land plants. Jawless fishes continued.
late-ordovician.ending: It ends at 443.1 Ma in the end-Ordovician mass extinction.

sandbian.etymology: Named for Sandby in south Sweden.
sandbian.climate: Warm, high seas. The Taconic orogeny was active in eastern North America.
sandbian.life: Graptolite zones become the global clock. Shelly faunas of brachiopods and trilobites were at their Ordovician richest.
sandbian.ending: It ends at 452.8 Ma, the base of the Katian.

katian.etymology: Named for Katy Lake, near the type section in Oklahoma. The lake is gone; the name remains.
katian.climate: Still warm for most of the age, with vast epicontinental seas. Cooling began near the end as ice gathered on Gondwana.
katian.life: The gallery trilobites of about 450 Ma, including Isotelus, belong here, among crinoid gardens in the seas that covered eastern North America.
katian.ending: It ends at 445.2 Ma at the base of the Hirnantian, on the brink of the glaciation.

hirnantian.etymology: Named for Cwm Hirnant in north Wales. It is short, and it holds the end-Ordovician mass extinction.
hirnantian.climate: Ice sheets on Gondwana pulled sea level down by tens of metres. Shallow tropical shelves were exposed, then flooded again as the ice melted.
hirnantian.life: A cold-water Hirnantia brachiopod fauna spread worldwide, then collapsed. Graptolites, many trilobites, and the reef builders were devastated.
hirnantian.ending: It ends at 443.1 Ma. About 85 percent of marine species died across the two pulses of this extinction. The Silurian begins on the far side.

llandovery.etymology: Named for Llandovery, a town in Carmarthenshire, Wales.
llandovery.climate: The ice melted, seas rose, and the climate warmed quickly after the Hirnantian. Reefs were gone and had to be rebuilt.
llandovery.life: Graptolites rediversified and became the zone fossils. Early vascular plants, including Cooksonia, appear in this epoch. Jawed fishes are known from a few fossils.
llandovery.ending: It ends at 432.9 Ma, the base of the Wenlock.

rhuddanian.climate: Post-glacial warming and a rising sea. The shelves were still ecologically thin after the extinction.
rhuddanian.life: A recovery fauna of graptolites and brachiopods. Diversity was low compared with the middle of the Silurian.

aeronian.climate: Warming continued and carbonate shelves returned in the tropics.
aeronian.life: Graptolite diversity climbed. The first good records of small vascular plants on land fall in this age.

telychian.etymology: Named for Pen-lan-Telych, a farm near Llandovery.
telychian.climate: A warm greenhouse peak within the Silurian, with widespread reefs starting to regrow.
telychian.life: Conodonts and graptolites both diverse. Early jawed vertebrates are present. Land plants remained small and tied to wet ground.
telychian.ending: It ends at 432.9 Ma, the base of the Sheinwoodian.

wenlock.etymology: Named for Wenlock Edge in Shropshire, a famous limestone scarp.
wenlock.climate: Warm, high seas and the return of large reefs built by corals and stromatoporoid sponges.
wenlock.life: Reef communities were rich again. Sea scorpions were large predators. The oldest fairly complete jawed fishes turn up in rocks of this epoch.

sheinwoodian.etymology: Named for Sheinwood, a hamlet in Shropshire.
sheinwoodian.climate: Warm shallow seas. A carbon-isotope excursion, the Ireviken event, marks a small extinction among conodonts and trilobites at the base.
sheinwoodian.life: After that hitch, reef life flourished. Graptolites were reduced in deeper water and shelly faunas took over the geological clock.

homerian.etymology: Named for Homer, a place in Shropshire, not the poet.
homerian.climate: Warm seas continued. A smaller biotic event, the Mulde excursion, sits near the middle of the age.
homerian.life: Coral-stromatoporoid reefs and brachiopod banks. The first certain air-breathing animals are debated, but millipede-like trackways are this old.
homerian.ending: It ends at 426.7 Ma, the base of the Gorstian.

ludlow.etymology: Named for the town of Ludlow, Shropshire. On this chart it runs from 426.7 to 422.7 Ma, and the undivided Přídolí follows it.
ludlow.climate: Warm climate, extensive carbonate platforms, and the continuing collision that would become the Caledonian mountains.
ludlow.life: Reefs, brachiopods, and a growing record of jawed fishes, including early acanthodians and placoderms. Land plants were still only centimetres tall.
ludlow.ending: It ends at 422.7 Ma, the base of the Přídolí.

gorstian.etymology: Named for Gorsty Farm near Ludlow.
gorstian.climate: Warm shelves. Sea level was relatively high at the start and then fell a little.
gorstian.life: A continuation of the Wenlock reef fauna. Graptolites were fewer and mostly in offshore water.

ludfordian.etymology: Named for Ludford, a village beside Ludlow.
ludfordian.climate: A short age with a notable carbon-isotope spike, the Lau event, tied to a turnover in conodonts.
ludfordian.life: Reefs stumbled during the Lau event and then recovered. Fishes with jaws were becoming more common in marginal seas.

pridoli.etymology: Named for Přídolí, near Prague. It is an epoch that the chart does not divide into ages.
pridoli.climate: Warm, and in places a falling sea as the Devonian approached. The Caledonian mountains were rising between Laurentia and Baltica.
pridoli.life: The first forests were still in the future, but small plants and arthropods were established on land. In the sea, the fauna grades smoothly into the early Devonian.
pridoli.ending: It ends at 419.62 Ma at the golden spike of the Devonian, drawn on a graptolite.

early-devonian.etymology: The Early Devonian. Its base is the Silurian–Devonian golden spike at 419.62 Ma.
early-devonian.climate: Warm and often arid on land. Sea level rose through the epoch. Euramerica was assembling.
early-devonian.life: Jawed fishes diversified quickly. Vascular plants crept inland from the coasts. The first ammonoids appear in the later part of the epoch.

lochkovian.etymology: Named for Lochkov in Prague, in the Czech Republic.
lochkovian.climate: A warm start to the Devonian, with widespread shallow seas over Europe.
lochkovian.life: Graptolites were almost gone. Early ammonoids had not yet appeared. Fishes and brachiopods dominate the fossil record.

pragian.climate: A short, warm age. Continental red beds in Britain record dry coastal plains.
pragian.life: The Rhynie Chert of Scotland, a hot-spring wetland with early plants and arthropods, is about this age. It is our best window on early land life.
pragian.ending: It ends at 410.62 Ma, after less than three million years.

emsian.etymology: Named for Bad Ems in Germany.
emsian.climate: Warm, with rising seas. Mountain building continued in the Caledonides.
emsian.life: Ammonoids appear. Placoderm fishes became large and varied. Plants with leaves and deeper roots were spreading beyond the wetlands.
emsian.ending: It ends at 393.47 Ma, the base of the Eifelian.

middle-devonian.etymology: The Middle Devonian, a high point for reefs and for fishes.
middle-devonian.climate: Greenhouse warmth and high sea level. Huge reef tracts grew in Canada, Australia, and Europe.
middle-devonian.life: Placoderms, early sharks, and lobe-finned fishes. The first trees, of the genus Wattieza, and the oldest known forests.

eifelian.etymology: Named for the Eifel hills of Germany.
eifelian.climate: Warm shallow seas and the start of the great Devonian reef systems.
eifelian.life: A rich brachiopod and coral fauna. The Kačák event, a black-shale pulse near the end, marks a small extinction.

givetian.etymology: Named for Givet in northern France.
givetian.climate: Peak reef growth and a warm, high sea. The Taghanic event near the end is a pulse of extinction and a fall of sea level.
givetian.life: Armored fishes were diverse. Forests of cladoxylopsid trees were established. The first tetrapod-like fishes are close in time.
givetian.ending: It ends at 382.31 Ma, the base of the Frasnian.

late-devonian.etymology: The Late Devonian, the epoch of Tiktaalik and of the extinction that ended the Age of Fishes as it had been.
late-devonian.climate: Still warm at the start. Reefs were vast, then collapsed. Black shales spread, a sign of oxygen-poor seas. By the end, ice may have returned on Gondwana.
late-devonian.life: Placoderms such as Dunkleosteus, lobe-fins including Tiktaalik, and the first amphibians. Archaeopteris forests shaded the floodplains.
late-devonian.ending: It ends at 358.86 Ma. Two extinctions define it: the Kellwasser crisis at 372.15 Ma and the Hangenberg crisis at the very end.

frasnian.climate: Warm seas and the last flourishing of the great Devonian reefs. Oxygen-poor water repeatedly spilled onto the shelves.
frasnian.life: Dunkleosteus and other giant placoderms. Tiktaalik, about 375 Ma, propped itself in river deltas of what is now Arctic Canada. Reefs of stromatoporoids and corals were at their peak.
frasnian.ending: It ends at 372.15 Ma in the Kellwasser event, the main pulse of the Late Devonian mass extinction. Reefs died and many fish groups were cut down.

famennian.etymology: Named for the Famenne region of Belgium.
famennian.climate: After the reefs collapsed, the seas were poorer and at times short of oxygen. A glaciation on Gondwana arrived at the very end.
famennian.life: Survivors included smaller placoderms, early sharks, and the first tetrapods with digits. Dunkleosteus persisted into this age. Forests of Archaeopteris still stood.
famennian.ending: It ends at 358.86 Ma in the Hangenberg event, a second extinction that removed the last placoderms and marks the base of the Carboniferous.

mississippian.etymology: Named for the Mississippi Valley, where the limestone of this subperiod is thick. In the United States the Carboniferous is split this way; many other regions say Early Carboniferous.
mississippian.climate: Warm seas covered much of North America and Europe with limestone. Ice was beginning to grow on Gondwana, and sea level started its glacial rises and falls.
mississippian.life: Crinoid meadows and diverse sharks. On land, the first extensive forests and the first reptiles were just getting started. Amphibians were the large land animals.
mississippian.ending: It ends at 323.4 Ma at the base of the Pennsylvanian.

early-mississippian.etymology: The Tournaisian age, the whole of the Early Mississippian on this chart.
early-mississippian.climate: A warm transgression laid down widespread limestone after the Devonian extinctions.
early-mississippian.life: A recovery fauna. Crinoids and brachiopods refilled the shelves. Fishes were mostly sharks and ray-fins after the placoderms vanished.

tournaisian.climate: Warm, high seas and a limestone world. The Hangenberg extinction was only just over.
tournaisian.life: Crinoid forests on the seafloor, surviving tetrapods in the rivers, and the slow return of reefs.
tournaisian.ending: It ends at 346.7 Ma, the base of the Visean. On this chart the age and the epoch have the same bounds.

middle-mississippian.etymology: The Visean age fills this whole epoch on the chart.
middle-mississippian.climate: Warm and humid in the tropics. Coal swamps were starting. Gondwanan ice was growing.
middle-mississippian.life: The first large coal-swamp plants, vast crinoid and bryozoan banks, and a richer tetrapod fauna.

visean.etymology: Named for Visé in Belgium. The chart spells it Visean.
visean.climate: Tropical humidity and the first true coal measures in places. Sea level pulsed as ice in the south waxed and waned.
visean.life: Lycopod trees became common. Amphibians were diverse. The oldest reptiles may date from the later Visean.

late-mississippian.etymology: The Serpukhovian age. Its base does not yet have a ratified golden spike.
late-mississippian.climate: Ice on Gondwana was substantial, and sea level was restless. Tropical coal swamps expanded.
late-mississippian.life: A rich shark fauna, including strange tooth-whorl forms related to later Helicoprion. Tetrapods continued in the wetlands.

serpukhovian.etymology: Named for Serpukhov, south of Moscow.
serpukhovian.climate: A cooler swing within the Carboniferous, with falling sea level in many basins.
serpukhovian.life: Crinoids and brachiopods were still abundant. A notable extinction of crinoids sits near the end of the age.
serpukhovian.ending: It ends at 323.4 Ma at the base of the Bashkirian. The golden spike for this base is not yet ratified.

pennsylvanian.etymology: Named for Pennsylvania, the classic coal country of this subperiod.
pennsylvanian.climate: The great tropical coal swamps of Euramerica. Oxygen was high, and glacial cycles on Gondwana made sea level swing again and again.
pennsylvanian.life: Scale trees, giant arthropods such as Meganeura and Arthropleura, and the first abundant amniotes in the drier parts of the landscape.
pennsylvanian.ending: It ends at 298.9 Ma at the base of the Permian.

early-pennsylvanian.etymology: The Bashkirian age fills the epoch.
early-pennsylvanian.climate: Coal swamps established themselves across the equator. Glacio-eustatic cycles are already clear in the rock record.
early-pennsylvanian.life: Lycopod forests and a growing fauna of large insects and amphibians.

bashkirian.etymology: Named for Bashkiria in the southern Urals.
bashkirian.climate: Humid tropics and a high-oxygen atmosphere beginning to support very large arthropods.
bashkirian.life: Coal-swamp floras and the earliest well-known amniote trackways in some regions.
bashkirian.ending: It ends at 315.2 Ma. The top is not fixed by a golden spike.

middle-pennsylvanian.etymology: The Moscovian age. Its base awaits a golden spike.
middle-pennsylvanian.climate: Peak coal-swamp conditions in many Euramerican basins, with strong glacial cycles.
middle-pennsylvanian.life: The classic Carboniferous wetland fauna: large amphibians, early reptiles, and giant arthropods in the standing forests.

moscovian.climate: Warm, wet tropics beside a glaciated south. Cyclothems, the repeating rock bundles of swamp and sea, are characteristic.
moscovian.life: Ferns, horsetails, and scale trees. Insects were diverse and some were already very large.

late-pennsylvanian.etymology: Kasimovian and Gzhelian together. The coal forests were still vast, but drier habitats were spreading.
late-pennsylvanian.climate: Continued glacial cycles. The Variscan mountains were rising in Europe as Gondwana pushed into Euramerica.
late-pennsylvanian.life: Meganeura, with a wingspan of about 70 centimetres, and the millipede Arthropleura, about two metres long, lived in these swamps around 305 Ma.
late-pennsylvanian.ending: It ends at 298.9 Ma as the climate tipped toward the drier Permian.

kasimovian.etymology: Named for Kasimov in Russia. The base is not yet a golden spike.
kasimovian.climate: Coal swamps under a high-oxygen sky, with ice still on Gondwana.
kasimovian.life: The gallery scenes of Meganeura and Arthropleura, about 305 Ma, fall in this age. Amphibians and the early synapsids shared the levees.

gzhelian.etymology: Named for Gzhel, a village near Moscow.
gzhelian.climate: The last Carboniferous coal forests, already shrinking in places as the climate dried.
gzhelian.life: A continuation of the swamp fauna, with reptiles and synapsids becoming more common away from the water.
gzhelian.ending: It ends at 298.9 Ma, the base of the Permian, at a golden spike in Kazakhstan.

cisuralian.etymology: From the Latin for this side of the Urals, the western slope, where the epoch was defined.
cisuralian.climate: Gondwanan ice was melting. Pangaea was nearly complete and its interior was turning dry and seasonal.
cisuralian.life: The sail-backed synapsid Dimetrodon in the red beds of Texas, and the buzz-saw shark Helicoprion in the seas. Amphibians were still important.
cisuralian.ending: It ends at 274.4 Ma, the base of the Roadian.

asselian.etymology: Named for the Assel River in the southern Urals.
asselian.climate: A drying trend from the coal swamps, with remaining ice on the southern continents.
asselian.life: Marine faunas of brachiopods and fusulinid foraminifera. On land, the first Permian tetrapod communities.

sakmarian.etymology: Named for the Sakmara River in the Urals.
sakmarian.climate: Ice was retreating. Red beds and evaporites record dry continental interiors.
sakmarian.life: A rich fusulinid and brachiopod sea. Tetrapod faunas of the early Permian style were established.

artinskian.etymology: Named for Artinsk in the Urals.
artinskian.climate: Warming and drying. The red floodplains of north Texas are the classic landscape.
artinskian.life: Dimetrodon, a synapsid closer to mammals than to reptiles, basked on those floodplains about 285 Ma. It is the animal in the gallery, sail and all.
artinskian.ending: It ends at 283.3 Ma. The top is not a ratified golden spike.

kungurian.etymology: Named for Kungur in the Urals.
kungurian.climate: Increasing aridity. Salt deposits are common. The last scraps of the great southern ice were melting.
kungurian.life: Helicoprion, the shark relative with a spiral tooth whorl, swam in seas of this age, about 280 Ma. On land, synapsids remained the large predators.
kungurian.ending: It ends at 274.4 Ma at the base of the Roadian.

guadalupian.etymology: Named for the Guadalupe Mountains of Texas and New Mexico, where the epoch's golden spikes are set.
guadalupian.climate: A warm world with a huge tropical reef complex, the Capitan reef, ringing the Delaware Basin. The Pangaean interior was desert.
guadalupian.life: Therapsids, the synapsids that include the ancestors of mammals, diversified. In the sea, brachiopods, ammonoids, and reefs were rich until a crisis at the end.
guadalupian.ending: It ends at 259.51 Ma in the Capitanian extinction, a severe warming and extinction just before the larger disaster at the end of the Permian.

roadian.etymology: Named for the Road Canyon Formation in the Guadalupe Mountains.
roadian.climate: Warm, with the Capitan reef system growing. Continental climates were strongly seasonal.
roadian.life: A turnover in brachiopods and ammonoids at the base. Therapsids were spreading on land.

wordian.etymology: Named for the Word Formation in the Guadalupe Mountains.
wordian.climate: Peak development of the Permian reef. The climate stayed hot and, inland, dry.
wordian.life: Rich sponge and brachiopod reefs. Dinocephalian therapsids were among the large land animals.

capitanian.etymology: Named for Capitan Peak in the Guadalupe Mountains.
capitanian.climate: The great reef reached its greatest size, then the climate warmed sharply at the end.
capitanian.life: A diverse reef fauna and, on land, the last of several early therapsid groups. The extinction at the end hit the reefs and the dinocephalians.
capitanian.ending: It ends at 259.51 Ma in the Capitanian, or end-Guadalupian, extinction, a prelude to the end-Permian crisis.

lopingian.etymology: Named for Leping in Jiangxi, China.
lopingian.climate: Hot, and in the last million years disrupted by the Siberian Traps, a vast volcanic province in what is now Siberia.
lopingian.life: A last flourishing of brachiopods, ammonoids, and trilobites, and on land the dicynodonts and gorgonopsian predators. Diversity was already fragile.
lopingian.ending: It ends at 251.902 Ma in the end-Permian mass extinction, the largest known.

wuchiapingian.etymology: Named for Wuchiaping in Shaanxi, China.
wuchiapingian.climate: Hot greenhouse conditions. The ocean was beginning to show stress before the final eruptions.
wuchiapingian.life: A recovery from the Capitanian extinction, with new brachiopod and ammonoid faunas. Dicynodonts were common herbivores.

changhsingian.etymology: Named for Changxing in Zhejiang, China, where the golden spike of the Triassic is also defined, just above.
changhsingian.climate: The Siberian Traps erupted through coal and salt, loading the air with carbon dioxide and halogens. The oceans warmed, acidified, and lost their oxygen.
changhsingian.life: The last trilobites, most brachiopods, the tabulate and rugose corals, and most land vertebrates died. A few lineages, including the dicynodonts that would become Lystrosaurus, scraped through.
changhsingian.ending: It ends at 251.902 Ma. Roughly 80 to 90 percent of marine species disappeared. The Paleozoic ends with this age.

early-triassic.etymology: The recovery interval after the end-Permian extinction. It is short by Paleozoic standards.
early-triassic.climate: The planet stayed extremely hot for a long time. Tropical oceans were often too hot and too low in oxygen for diverse life. Pangaea was intact and dry.
early-triassic.life: Disaster faunas. Lystrosaurus, a burrowing dicynodont, spread across Pangaea. In the sea, a few molluscs and stromatolites, which had a brief comeback, dominated.
early-triassic.ending: It ends at 246.7 Ma, the base of the Anisian, as diversity finally started to rebuild.

induan.etymology: Named for the Indus River. It is the first Triassic age, and it is only about two million years long.
induan.climate: Scorched, with repeated oxygen crises in the sea. Red beds and sparse fossils are typical.
induan.life: Lystrosaurus in the Karoo of South Africa, about 250 Ma, is the gallery animal of this age. Little else was large.

olenekian.etymology: Named for the Olenek River in Siberia. The golden spike is not yet ratified.
olenekian.climate: Still hot, with a notable further warming and extinction pulse, the Smithian-Spathian crisis, in the middle of the age.
olenekian.life: The first ichthyosaurs took to the sea. Land communities remained thin, though archosaurs were beginning to diversify.

middle-triassic.etymology: The Middle Triassic. Life was finally building complex ecosystems again. The top, about 237 Ma, is approximate.
middle-triassic.climate: Still warm and still Pangaea, but the oceans were habitable again and carbonate platforms returned.
middle-triassic.life: Marine reptiles diversified. On land, the archosaurs that include crocodile-line animals and the first dinosaurs were rising. Conifer forests spread.
middle-triassic.ending: It ends near 237 Ma at the base of the Carnian.

anisian.etymology: Named from Anisus, the Latin name of the Enns River in the Alps. The golden spike is not yet ratified.
anisian.climate: Warm shallow seas returned to the Tethys, the ocean between the northern and southern arms of Pangaea.
anisian.life: The recovery of reefs and of ammonoids. Early archosaurs and the relatives of dinosaurs become common fossils.

ladinian.etymology: Named for the Ladin people of the Dolomites.
ladinian.climate: Warm, with spectacular carbonate platforms in the Dolomites of Italy. The top of the age is still approximate.
ladinian.life: Marine reptiles, including the first nothosaur-type swimmers, and a land fauna in which the dinosaur line was present but not yet dominant.

late-triassic.etymology: The Late Triassic. Dinosaurs went from rare to widespread, and the epoch ends in a mass extinction. The base, about 237 Ma, is approximate.
late-triassic.climate: Hot and seasonal. Rifts that would become the Atlantic were starting to stretch Pangaea. There was no polar ice.
late-triassic.life: Early dinosaurs, the first mammals, pterosaurs by the end, and huge crocodile-line predators. Conifers, cycads, and ferns.
late-triassic.ending: It ends at 201.4 Ma in the end-Triassic extinction.

carnian.etymology: Named for the Carnic Alps. Both bounds are approximate on the chart.
carnian.climate: A wet episode, the Carnian Pluvial Event, broke the usual aridity for a million years or so and may have helped dinosaurs spread.
carnian.life: The first abundant dinosaurs appear during and after that wet spell. Early turtles and the first mammals are Carnian as well.

norian.etymology: Named for Noricum, the Roman province in the Alps. The bounds are approximate, and the golden spike is not ratified.
norian.climate: A return to hot, dry Pangaean climates, with a long and relatively stable interval.
norian.life: Dinosaurs became the dominant large herbivores in many regions. Pterosaurs flew. The first ichthyosaurs of more familiar shape were in the sea.

rhaetian.etymology: Named for the Rhaetian Alps. The base is approximate and has no golden spike yet.
rhaetian.climate: Rifting quickened. The Central Atlantic Magmatic Province began to erupt as the age closed, pumping carbon dioxide into the air.
rhaetian.life: A last Triassic fauna of plated dinosaurs, large amphibians, and conodonts in the sea. Many of these groups end here.
rhaetian.ending: It ends at 201.4 Ma. Conodonts died out for good, and the large crocodile-line archosaurs lost the land to the dinosaurs. The Jurassic begins.

early-jurassic.etymology: The Early Jurassic, after the end-Triassic extinction had cleared the large land predators.
early-jurassic.climate: Pangaea was breaking. The climate was warmer and wetter than the Triassic, and shallow seas began to flood Europe.
early-jurassic.life: Dinosaurs diversified into the roles left open. Marine reptiles recovered. Ammonites became the standard zone fossils.

hettangian.climate: A warm recovery interval. The new Atlantic rift was still narrow.
hettangian.life: A thinned fauna just after the extinction. Ammonites of a few families, and on land the dinosaurs that had survived.
hettangian.ending: It ends at 199.5 Ma, after less than two million years.

sinemurian.etymology: Named for Sinemurum, the Latin name of Semur-en-Auxois in France.
sinemurian.climate: Warm, with spreading shallow seas over Europe.
sinemurian.life: Ammonites diversified and became reliable clocks. Ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs were established in the seaways.

pliensbachian.climate: Continued warmth, with a notable cooling and extinction pulse near the end, in the late Pliensbachian.
pliensbachian.life: Rich ammonite and belemnite faunas. Dinosaurs of the early Jurassic style, including early sauropods, were widespread.

toarcian.climate: A sharp warming at the base, the Toarcian Oceanic Anoxic Event, when oxygen-poor seas laid down black shale across Europe.
toarcian.life: A small extinction of marine life at that event, then a recovery. On land, sauropods and early theropods continued.
toarcian.ending: It ends at 174.7 Ma, the base of the Aalenian.

middle-jurassic.etymology: The Middle Jurassic. Dinosaurs were large, and the Atlantic was a real ocean.
middle-jurassic.climate: Warm and humid. Sea level was rising. Carbonate platforms and sponge reefs grew in the Tethys.
middle-jurassic.life: The first truly huge sauropods, and large pliosaurs such as Liopleurodon in the European seas.

aalenian.climate: A warm, relatively short age with spreading seas.
aalenian.life: Ammonites of the graphoceratid groups mark the zones. Marine reptiles and dinosaurs of the Middle Jurassic style were in place.

bajocian.etymology: Named for Bayeux in Normandy, whose Latin name was Bajocae.
bajocian.climate: Warm shelves and the growth of oolitic limestones across Europe.
bajocian.life: A diverse ammonite fauna. Sauropods were the dominant large herbivores on several continents.

bathonian.etymology: Named for Bath, England, a city built of this limestone.
bathonian.climate: Warm, high seas. The oolites of Bath are hardened lime sand from these tropical shallows.
bathonian.life: Dinosaurs known from good skeletons, including early stegosaurs in some regions. Plesiosaurs were common offshore.

callovian.etymology: Named for Kellaways in Wiltshire. The name was coined from the Latinized place name. The golden spike is not yet ratified.
callovian.climate: Warm shallow seas covered much of Europe, with sponge reefs below the storm waves.
callovian.life: Liopleurodon, the big-headed pliosaur in the gallery, hunted these seas. Ammonites are abundant enough that the age is finely zoned.
callovian.ending: It ends at 161.5 Ma, the base of the Oxfordian and of the Late Jurassic.

late-jurassic.etymology: The Late Jurassic, the time of the Morrison Formation and of Archaeopteryx. The base has no ratified golden spike.
late-jurassic.climate: Warm, and in places arid on the American plains. A seaway covered much of Europe. The Atlantic was open in the middle but not yet in the south.
late-jurassic.life: Stegosaurus, Allosaurus, Archaeopteryx, ichthyosaurs, and a great diversity of ammonites.
late-jurassic.ending: It ends at 143.1 Ma. The boundary with the Cretaceous is an estimate, not a golden spike.

oxfordian.climate: Warm seas over Europe and a mosaic of rivers and dry plains in western North America.
oxfordian.life: Ophthalmosaurus, the big-eyed ichthyosaur in the gallery, hunted ammonites about 160 Ma. Pliosaurs were still the top predators.

kimmeridgian.etymology: Named for Kimmeridge, a village on the Dorset coast.
kimmeridgian.climate: Warm, with a productive sea that laid down the organic-rich Kimmeridge Clay, a major oil source.
kimmeridgian.life: The Morrison Formation's Stegosaurus, about this age, browsed fern prairies in western North America. Ammonites and marine reptiles filled the European sea.

tithonian.etymology: Named for Tithonus, a figure of Greek myth, the husband of Eos, the dawn, because the age sits at the dawn of the Cretaceous. The golden spike is not ratified.
tithonian.climate: Warm lagoons and arid plains. The Solnhofen lagoons of Bavaria were hypersaline backwaters of the Tethys.
tithonian.life: Archaeopteryx lived on those lagoon shores. The oldest Solnhofen beds sit near the Kimmeridgian boundary on this chart, and the bird is conventionally treated as Tithonian.
tithonian.ending: It ends at 143.1 Ma, the working age of the Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary.

early-cretaceous.etymology: The Early Cretaceous. There is no Middle Cretaceous on the chart. The base, 143.1 Ma, is not a golden spike.
early-cretaceous.climate: Continents were still splitting. The climate was a warm greenhouse with some cooler spells. Seas gradually rose.
early-cretaceous.life: Dinosaurs of a new cast: spinosaurids were coming, flowering plants appeared, and birds became more modern. Iguanodon and its relatives were widespread herbivores.
early-cretaceous.ending: It ends at 100.5 Ma, the base of the Cenomanian.

berriasian.etymology: Named for Berrias in southern France. The golden spike at the base is not ratified, which is why the Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary is still open.
berriasian.climate: Warm, with lagoon and lake deposits common in Europe. Sea level was lower than it would be later in the Cretaceous.
berriasian.life: A dinosaur fauna still close to the Late Jurassic. Ammonites were rebuilding after a turnover at the boundary.

valanginian.climate: A cooler pulse within the greenhouse, the Valanginian Weissert event, with a carbon-isotope shift.
valanginian.life: Early Cretaceous dinosaurs and the first widely discussed flowering-plant fossils near the end of this stretch of time.

hauterivian.climate: Warm, with rising seas. Patagonia was a land of braided rivers and conifer forests.
hauterivian.life: Amargasaurus, the spined sauropod in the gallery, lived in Neuquén about 129 Ma, which on this chart falls in the Hauterivian.

barremian.climate: Warm, and in places a slight fall of sea level. Lake basins in China preserved exceptional fossils.
barremian.life: The Jehol biota of Liaoning, with feathered dinosaurs and early birds, is about this age. Flowering plants were present but not yet dominant.

aptian.etymology: Named for Apt in France. The base is not yet a golden spike.
aptian.climate: A very warm age, with ocean anoxic events that laid down black shale. Sea level was rising toward the Cretaceous maximum.
aptian.life: Deinonychus hunted in the conifer and fern forests of what is now Montana, about 115 Ma. Early flowering plants spread. Sauropods were still major herbivores in the southern continents.

albian.etymology: Named for the Aube, Alba in Latin, a region of France.
albian.climate: Seas rose toward the highest stand of the Mesozoic. The climate was hot. Chalk and greensand are typical sediments.
albian.life: A diverse dinosaur fauna worldwide, ichthyosaurs in their last ages, and flowering plants becoming ecologically important.
albian.ending: It ends at 100.5 Ma at the base of the Cenomanian, a major turnover in ammonites and the start of the Late Cretaceous.

late-cretaceous.etymology: The Late Cretaceous, the classic dinosaur world of Hell Creek, the chalk seas, and the Western Interior Seaway.
late-cretaceous.climate: Greenhouse heat and very high sea level. North America was split by a seaway. There was little or no polar ice, and forests grew at high latitudes.
late-cretaceous.life: Tyrannosaurs, horned dinosaurs, hadrosaurs, giant azhdarchid pterosaurs, mosasaurs, and ammonites. Flowering plants and broad-leaved trees were common.
late-cretaceous.ending: It ends at 66 Ma in the end-Cretaceous mass extinction.

cenomanian.etymology: Named for Cenomanum, the Latin name of Le Mans.
cenomanian.climate: The sea rose to one of its highest stands. A major oxygen crisis, Oceanic Anoxic Event 2, sits at the end of the age.
cenomanian.life: Spinosaurus hunted rivers in the Kem Kem of North Africa about 95 Ma. Ammonites and rudists, strange reef-building clams, flourished until the anoxic event.
cenomanian.ending: It ends at 93.9 Ma. The anoxic event caused a real extinction in the sea, though it is not one of the Big Five.

turonian.climate: Peak Cretaceous sea level and heat, just after the anoxic event.
turonian.life: Mosasaurs were becoming the new top marine predators as ichthyosaurs faded. Dinosaurs continued on the remaining land.

coniacian.etymology: Named for Cognac, France, Coniacum in Latin.
coniacian.climate: Still a high, warm sea. The Western Interior Seaway was in place.
coniacian.life: A continuation of the Late Cretaceous fauna. Rudists built reefs in the tropics. Ammonites are the zone fossils.

santonian.climate: High sea level. Chalk was accumulating in Europe, and the Western Interior Seaway covered the Great Plains.
santonian.life: Pteranodon nested on the chalky shores of that seaway about 85 Ma, which is the gallery colony. The genus also ranges into the Campanian.

campanian.etymology: Named for Champagne, Campania in Latin.
campanian.climate: The seaway was still broad. The climate stayed warm, with a slight cooling toward the end.
campanian.life: Archelon, the giant sea turtle in the gallery, swam the seaway about 75 Ma. Hadrosaurs and ceratopsians were diverse. Pteranodon still flew.

maastrichtian.etymology: Named for Maastricht in the Netherlands, where the type chalk was studied.
maastrichtian.climate: The Western Interior Seaway was shallowing. The climate was still warmer than today. The Deccan Traps in India began to erupt before the age ended.
maastrichtian.life: Tyrannosaurus, Triceratops, and Quetzalcoatlus, all in the gallery, lived in the last few million years. Ammonites and mosasaurs were still in the sea.
maastrichtian.ending: It ends at 66 Ma. The Chicxulub impact, and the Deccan eruptions, ended the non-bird dinosaurs, the pterosaurs, the ammonites, and the marine reptiles.

paleocene.etymology: Greek palaios and kainos, old-recent. It is the epoch just after the dinosaurs, and it ends in an extreme warming.
paleocene.climate: Cooler than the later Eocene at first, then warming. Continents were near their modern places. There were no large ice sheets.
paleocene.life: Mammals stayed small at first, then grew. Birds filled some of the predator roles. Forests recovered quickly after the impact.
paleocene.ending: It ends at 56.0 Ma in the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum, a sudden global warming.

danian.etymology: Named for Denmark, Dania, where the limestone was studied.
danian.climate: A world recovering from the impact. The climate was milder than the Late Cretaceous greenhouse but still warmer than today.
danian.life: A low-diversity recovery. Small mammals, surviving birds, and new plankton. Ferns briefly dominated some landscapes right after the impact, just before this age.

selandian.etymology: Named for Zealand, Sjælland, in Denmark.
selandian.climate: A cooler middle of the Paleocene, with falling sea level in some regions.
selandian.life: Mammals were diversifying into more distinct groups. Forests were widespread, including at high latitudes.

thanetian.etymology: Named for the Isle of Thanet in Kent.
thanetian.climate: Warming toward the end of the age, setting up the thermal maximum.
thanetian.life: Early primates, rodents, and the first larger plant-eating mammals. The seas held new lineages of plankton that still have descendants today.
thanetian.ending: It ends at 56.0 Ma at the carbon-isotope spike of the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum.

eocene.etymology: Greek eos and kainos, dawn of the recent. Charles Lyell named it for the dawn of modern marine faunas.
eocene.climate: The warmest stretch of the Cenozoic. Forests reached the Arctic. There was little ice until the very end, when Antarctica began to freeze.
eocene.life: The first horses, whales, bats, and elephants. Primates were widespread. Gastornis, a giant flightless bird, lived in the forests of what is now Wyoming.
eocene.ending: It ends at 33.9 Ma with a sharp cooling and the growth of the Antarctic ice sheet.

ypresian.climate: The Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum at the base, then a very warm climate. Crocodiles and palm forests reached high latitudes.
ypresian.life: Gastornis, about 52 Ma, in subtropical Wyoming. Early horses the size of foxes. The first fully aquatic whales appear near the end of the age.

lutetian.climate: Still a warm greenhouse. India was closing on Asia, and the Tethys was narrowing.
lutetian.life: Andrewsarchus, known from a huge skull in Inner Mongolia, lived about 45 Ma on these warm floodplains. Whales such as the ancestors of Basilosaurus were taking to the sea.

bartonian.etymology: Named for Barton-on-Sea in Hampshire. The golden spike is not yet ratified.
bartonian.climate: Warm, but with the first signs of cooling from the early Eocene peak.
bartonian.life: Large mammals of the middle Eocene, and archaeocete whales in the Tethys. The gallery's Basilosaurus range of 40 to 34 Ma starts in this age.

priabonian.climate: Cooling toward the Eocene–Oligocene boundary. The first significant Antarctic ice arrived as the age closed.
priabonian.life: Basilosaurus, an early whale up to about 18 metres long, cruised the Tethys in what is now Egypt. The famous Fayum whales are this age.
priabonian.ending: It ends at 33.9 Ma in a major cooling, a turnover of mammals in Europe called the Grande Coupure, and the start of a lasting Antarctic ice sheet.

oligocene.etymology: Greek oligos and kainos, few recent, because Lyell found only a few modern marine species in its rocks.
oligocene.climate: Cooler and drier than the Eocene. Antarctica carried ice. Grasslands and open woodland spread at the expense of closed forest.
oligocene.life: A more modern mammal fauna. Paraceratherium, among the largest land mammals ever, browsed in Asia. Early apes and monkeys were present.

rupelian.etymology: Named for the Rupel River in Belgium.
rupelian.climate: Cooler, with Antarctic ice. Open woodlands replaced many of the Eocene rainforests.
rupelian.life: Paraceratherium, the giant hornless rhinoceros in the gallery, lived in Central Asia about 30 Ma. Oreodonts and early horses were common in North America.

chattian.etymology: Named for the Chatti, a people of Roman-age Germany.
chattian.climate: A slight warming from the early Oligocene, then renewed cooling toward the Miocene. Ice remained on Antarctica.
chattian.life: Mammal faunas continued to modernize. In Africa, early relatives of elephants and the ancestors of apes were diversifying.
chattian.ending: It ends at 23.04 Ma, the base of the Miocene and of the Neogene.

miocene.etymology: Greek meion and kainos, less recent. Lyell's name for a fauna with fewer modern species than the Pliocene.
miocene.climate: Warmer than the Oligocene at first, then a steady cooling. Grasslands spread. The Mediterranean dried near the end. The Himalaya was rising.
miocene.life: Apes diversified. Horses became grazers. Deinotherium, Chalicotherium, and the shovel-tusked Platybelodon lived in the woodlands and wetlands.
miocene.ending: It ends at 5.333 Ma as the Mediterranean refilled at the start of the Pliocene.

aquitanian.climate: A warm early Miocene, wetter than the late Oligocene in many places.
aquitanian.life: A radiation of mammals into more modern families. Early apes were established in Africa and were spreading.
aquitanian.ending: It ends at 20.45 Ma. The chart puts the base at 23.04 Ma, the same age as the top of the Oligocene.

burdigalian.etymology: Named for Burdigala, Roman Bordeaux. The golden spike is not yet ratified.
burdigalian.climate: The Miocene climatic optimum was beginning: warmer than today, with forests expanding again.
burdigalian.life: Apes reached Eurasia. Proboscideans, the elephant family in the broad sense, spread out of Africa.

langhian.etymology: Named for the Langhe hills of Italy.
langhian.climate: The heart of the Miocene climatic optimum. Warm seas and a high sea level.
langhian.life: A rich marine fauna of the kind Lyell compared with the modern one. On land, horses and rhinos of open woodland.

serravallian.etymology: Named for Serravalle Scrivia in Italy.
serravallian.climate: Cooling began in earnest after the climatic optimum. The East Antarctic ice sheet expanded.
serravallian.life: Platybelodon, about 13 Ma, and Chalicotherium, about 12 Ma, both in the gallery, lived in the wetlands and forests of this age.

tortonian.climate: Continued cooling and drying. Grasslands expanded. The Himalaya was high enough to affect the monsoon.
tortonian.life: Deinotherium, the elephant relative with downward-curving lower tusks, browsed European riverbanks about 9 Ma. Apes were diverse in Eurasia.

messinian.climate: The Mediterranean largely dried up in the salinity crisis, leaving thick salt, then refilled when the Atlantic broke through at Gibraltar.
messinian.life: A drying world around that empty sea. Hominins in Africa were already separate from the other apes. Hipparion horses spread across the grasslands.
messinian.ending: It ends at 5.333 Ma with the Zanclean flood, when the Mediterranean refilled.

pliocene.etymology: Greek pleion and kainos, more recent.
pliocene.climate: Cooler and drier than the Miocene. The Isthmus of Panama closed, rerouting the oceans. Northern ice sheets were about to become permanent.
pliocene.life: A familiar mammal fauna: elephants, horses, cats, and in Africa the australopithecines. Marine faunas were close to modern.
pliocene.ending: It ends at 2.58 Ma at the start of the Quaternary ice ages.

zanclean.etymology: Named for Zancle, the old Greek name of Messina.
zanclean.climate: The Mediterranean was full again. The climate was warmer and wetter than the later Pliocene.
zanclean.life: Australopithecus appears in the later part of this age. Forests and woodlands were still broader than in the ice ages.

piacenzian.climate: Cooling toward the ice ages. The Panama isthmus was closed, and northern glaciation was intensifying.
piacenzian.life: The last of the warmer Pliocene faunas. Early species of Homo are close in time, just after this age on some chronologies.
piacenzian.ending: It ends at 2.58 Ma, the golden spike of the Gelasian and of the Quaternary.

pleistocene.etymology: Greek pleistos and kainos, most recent. Lyell named it for faunas in which most molluscs were still living species.
pleistocene.climate: Dozens of glacial and interglacial cycles. Ice sheets covered Canada and northern Europe in the cold stages. Sea level fell by more than 100 metres when the ice was large.
pleistocene.life: Mammoths, mastodons, ground sloths, sabre-toothed cats, and cave bears. Modern humans evolved in Africa and spread worldwide late in the epoch.
pleistocene.ending: It ends at 0.0117 Ma, 11,700 years ago, at the end of the last glacial period.

gelasian.etymology: Named for Gela in Sicily, near the golden spike at Monte San Nicola.
gelasian.climate: The first Quaternary age, when northern-hemisphere ice sheets became the main climate cycle.
gelasian.life: Early Pleistocene mammals, including the first mammoths of a more cold-adapted kind. Homo habilis and its relatives were in Africa.

calabrian.climate: Continued glacial cycles, generally a little less extreme than the later ones.
calabrian.life: Homo erectus spread out of Africa. Large mammals of the early Ice Age, including some of the last terror birds in the Americas.

chibanian.etymology: Named for Chiba Prefecture, Japan, where the golden spike is set in a deep-sea core.
chibanian.climate: The middle Pleistocene. Glacial cycles lengthened to about 100,000 years. Ice sheets were larger.
chibanian.life: Neanderthals and Denisovans emerged in Eurasia. Large mammals of the mammoth-steppe fauna were assembling.
chibanian.ending: It ends at 0.129 Ma, the start of the last interglacial.

late-pleistocene.etymology: An informal interval on the chart, the unnamed upper Pleistocene between the Chibanian and the Holocene. A formal stage name, Tarantian, has been proposed and is not ratified.
late-pleistocene.climate: The last interglacial, then the last glacial period, ending in the warming at 11,700 years ago. Ice covered Canada and Scandinavia at the maximum, about 20,000 years ago.
late-pleistocene.life: Woolly mammoths, Smilodon, cave bears, Irish elk, ground sloths, glyptodonts, and cave lions, all in the gallery. Modern humans reached the Americas and Australia. Many of the largest animals vanished as the ice melted.
late-pleistocene.ending: It ends at 0.0117 Ma. The warming into the Holocene, and human hunting, removed much of the remaining megafauna.

holocene.etymology: Greek holos and kainos, wholly recent. The current epoch, the one that began when the last glacial period ended.
holocene.climate: A relatively stable warm interval, compared with the Pleistocene swings. Sea level rose to about its present stand by the middle of the epoch. We are living in it.
holocene.life: The epoch of farming, cities, and the surviving Ice Age animals. A few megafauna, including the Wrangel Island mammoths, lasted into it. Living fossils in the gallery, such as coelacanths, nautiluses, tuatara, and horseshoe crabs, are shown as they live now. The pictures are AI reconstructions, not photographs.
holocene.ending: It has not ended. The chart runs it to the present, 0 Ma.

greenlandian.etymology: Named for the Greenland ice cores. The golden spike is in the NGRIP core, at the sharp warming that ends the Pleistocene.
greenlandian.climate: Rapid warming, rising seas, and the last of the great ice sheets wasting back. The Northgrippian cold snap was still ahead.
greenlandian.life: People were already farming in the Near East by the end of the age. Many Pleistocene megafauna were already gone.
greenlandian.ending: It ends at 0.0082 Ma, 8,200 years ago, at a sudden cooling recorded in the ice.

northgrippian.etymology: Named for the NorthGRIP ice core. The golden spike marks the 8.2-thousand-year cold event, when a pulse of meltwater chilled the North Atlantic.
northgrippian.climate: After that short cold snap, a warm and fairly stable climate. Sea level was close to today's.
northgrippian.life: Farming spread. The Irish elk lasted until about 7,700 years ago, inside this age, though the gallery shows it in an Ice Age setting.
northgrippian.ending: It ends at 0.0042 Ma, 4,200 years ago, at a widespread drought recorded in a cave in India.

meghalayan.etymology: Named for Meghalaya, India. The golden spike is a shift in oxygen isotopes in a stalagmite from Mawmluh Cave, marking a drought about 4,200 years ago.
meghalayan.climate: The current age. Climate has been broadly modern, with droughts, the Little Ice Age, and the warming of the last century. The continents and the shorelines are the ones on a present-day map.
meghalayan.life: The last Wrangel mammoths died about 4,000 years ago. Moa and Haast's eagle vanished after people reached New Zealand. The thylacine died in a zoo in 1936. Coelacanths, nautiluses, tuatara, and horseshoe crabs are alive now. The gallery's raptor, pterosaur, and dicynodont in modern forests are fiction.
meghalayan.ending: It has not ended. The top of the chart is today.
